title: Context Management in Coding Agents
thesis: Larger context windows did not make coding agents proportionally more reliable. The engineering problem is deciding what the agent should see, when it should see it, and what that context costs.
audience: For software and agent engineers working on multi-step repository tasks. Assumes comfort with tests, CI, APIs and production trade-offs.
description: Why more context can make coding agents less reliable, and what to do instead: ten methods, measured evidence, an evaluation design and a 16-hour plan.
summaryLede: Everything in this research on one page: the problem, the finding, the first actions, and the numbers behind them. Five minutes.
sourcesLede: What each source supports, how much to discount it, which chapters lean on it, and what would prove this research wrong.
methodLede: The research question, the design commitments fixed before writing, what is out of scope, and the acceptance bar the work had to pass.

summaryStats.label: tested across eight lengths; performance generally fell as input grew [S]
targeted retrieval beat a full codebase summary in one practitioner report [P]
SWE-bench swing from changing only the summariser [S]
Pass² with no compression vs FIFO truncation on AppWorld [S]
cost increase from a 24% token cut that broke the prompt cache [C]
practitioner estimate when dead or duplicate capabilities dominate; verify and keep rollback [P]

finding.claim: The context window is an attention budget, not a bucket.
finding.detail: Chroma tested 18 models across eight lengths and found performance generally degraded as input grew, with non-uniform, model-specific curves [S]. Correct but irrelevant tokens can still reduce performance.

finding.claim: Subtraction beats addition, and the evidence is lopsided.
finding.detail: 5K tokens of targeted retrieval beat a 100K summary [P]. Masking matched summarisation at lower cost [S]. Fewer tools beat more tools [S]. A first audit should test for waste before changing strategy.

finding.claim: Compression damage shows up as unreliability before it shows up as lower accuracy.
finding.detail: Compressed agents become intermittent: they solve a task, then fail the same task on a rerun [S]. Teams measuring single runs conclude compaction is free until production disagrees.

finding.claim: The cache can flip the sign of an optimisation.
finding.detail: In the worked price model, a 24% token cut that made the prefix dynamic raised cost 6.9× [C]. Token count alone is not a cost model.
About 16 hours of sequenced work, most of it deletion, covers the large majority of the benefit. Past the stop rule, your binding constraint is somewhere else.

chapters.title: Why more context can hurt coding agents
chapters.question: What is context, mechanically, and when does adding more make coding agents less reliable?
chapters.description: Context is an attention budget, not a container. The evidence for degradation, five constraints around a context decision, and five ways context fails.
tldr: Across Chroma's controlled tasks, performance generally fell as input grew, but the curves were model- and task-dependent [S].
Five constraints shape a context decision: dilution, position, recency bias in conflicts, cache and information loss.
Context fails in five ways. Starvation can leave no trace in the transcript, so it needs a read-coverage check.
outcomes: Explain the productive-band model without treating it as a universal curve
Route an observed symptom to one of five context constraints
Diagnose poisoning, distraction, confusion, clash and starvation from their tells
State the four properties of a well-managed context
takeaways: The window is an operating budget for useful signal. Adding correct information can still lower performance.
Position can change retrieval reliability, but the size and shape depend on model, task and harness.
Appending usually preserves the existing prefix; early edits can invalidate cached suffixes and may cost more than they save.
The programme's operating preference is reversibility over compression ratio: prefer operations you can undo.
You cannot delete from a transcript by talking to it. Reset instead of arguing.

see.title: Where the tokens actually go
see.why: the nine segments of a real context

chapters.title: Anatomy of a coding agent's context
chapters.question: Where do the tokens in a coding agent's context actually go, and which parts can you control?
chapters.description: Nine segments of a coding agent's context, their rough size, who controls them, how they fail, and a constructed worked budget that turns segment size into reversible actions.
tldr: A context has nine segments: four common prefix segments and five growing body segments.

In this audit model, prefix content is sent on every call; body content grows with the session, and cache billing depends on hits. Compaction or memory policy can rewrite or reposition body context [D].
The constructed audit finds its largest controllable segments in tool definitions and tool output.
outcomes: Split any context into prefix and body and explain why that split governs cost
Estimate the size, owner and failure mode of each of the nine segments
Rank clean-up actions by size, cost and reversibility
Track the four numbers that belong on a dashboard
takeaways: "My context is full" is not actionable. A segment-by-segment breakdown is.
In the constructed audit, tool definitions and tool results are the largest controllable segments.
Optimise the retention integral (tokens × turns kept), not the peak.
Compaction may rewrite earlier context, so treat it as cache-hostile until measured.
The worked audit ranks recoverable segments before behaviour-changing fixes; validate every change against task coverage [C].

chapters.title: Ten methods that survive scrutiny
chapters.question: Which context-management methods survive scrutiny, why does each work, and what does each cost?
chapters.description: Ten context-management methods for coding agents, each with its mechanism, cost, what it loses, how to detect trouble, and a test you can run today.
tldr: Only ten methods passed four tests: a mechanism, evidence, independence from the others, and a test you can run today.
Each method loses something. The loss mode matters as much as the gain.
The biggest wins are unglamorous: stable prefixes, fewer tools, and quieter tool output.
outcomes: Describe each of the ten methods in one sentence and name the force it acts on
State what each method costs and what it can lose
Run the decision test for any method on your own workload
Explain why popular advice such as bigger windows or default multi-agent was benched
takeaways: Measure your distribution before choosing any method.
Static pruning beats dynamic selection, mostly for cache reasons.
Never delete what you can relocate: redirect, offload, stub.
A plan file with a ruled-out section is the only deliberate control over what survives a boundary.
Compact at sub-goal boundaries, at most once, and only after offloading.

see.title: Choosing your methods
see.why: the 55-minute procedure that routes you to one

chapters.title: Choosing your methods: a 55-minute procedure
chapters.question: Given my own agent and workload, which method should I adopt first, and in what order after that?
chapters.description: An executable procedure with time budgets for choosing context-management methods: measure, route by binding constraint, classify the task, compose the stack.
tldr: Measure four numbers first. Every wrong context decision catalogued in this research started with a guess.
Route by your binding constraint and fix exactly one thing, then re-measure.
Three ordering rules are not optional: offload before compaction, state before resets, cache before everything.
outcomes: Produce the four routing numbers for your setup in 30 minutes
Pick your first method from the routing table
Adjust the stack for the task type in front of you
Answer the recurring 2 a.m. calls from the decision table
takeaways: The procedure is measure, route, classify, compose, then review quarterly.
Fix one constraint at a time so every effect stays attributable.
Different task types need different stacks; debugging and delegation do not mix.
Context management regresses. A 30-minute quarterly re-measure keeps it honest.

chapters.title: Retrieval: how code should enter context
chapters.question: Should code enter context by grep, embeddings, the symbol graph or agentic search, and what does the evidence actually say?
chapters.description: Lexical, structural, semantic and agentic retrieval compared on evidence, the harness confound, a tiered default architecture and nine code-specific pathologies.
tldr: "Grep versus embeddings" is the wrong question. Unit, index, timing and agency are separate choices.
The harness often matters more than the retrieval strategy, so published comparisons do not transfer [S].
Default: grep and the symbol graph first, semantic search only for unknown vocabulary, escalate rather than run everything.
outcomes: Decompose any retrieval design into unit, index, timing and agency
Choose a retrieval tier for a given question shape
Recognise the nine code-specific retrieval pathologies
Measure read-utilisation and read-coverage on your own agent
takeaways: Code has exact relevance edges. Use the compiler's graph before approximating it.
A method that fails loudly (zero hits) is safer than one that always returns something.
Pre-load pointers and invariants, never content, and keep the seed under 2,000 tokens.
Diagnose starvation versus dilution before changing retrieval volume.

chapters.title: Compaction, offload and memory
chapters.question: How do compaction, offload and memory lose information, what does that cost in measured terms, and what should you do with your wiki?
chapters.description: Six measured 2026 results on compaction, the design space, offload patterns, cross-session memory, and what a coding agent should do with your wiki, database and graph.
tldr: Changing only the summariser moved SWE-bench by 6.5 points. Compaction is a component, not plumbing [S].
Compression makes agents intermittent before it makes them worse on average [S].
Offload first, compact at boundaries, persist only what you would otherwise re-derive, and never bulk-index the wiki.
outcomes: Distinguish compaction, offload and memory by scope, reversibility and cost
Configure a compaction trigger, schema and cap from the evidence
Design self-describing offload stubs
Decide where a fact should live using its staleness rate
takeaways: Offload before you compact, and persist only what you would re-derive.
Use an explicit summary schema with state, ruled-out approaches and verbatim exact strings.
Re-read the plan file first after any compaction; that step carries the most errors.
The repository is the only store with a repair mechanism. Prefer ADRs and tests to memory tools.
Dereference the wiki by name; never index it.

chapters.title: Sub-agents and isolation
chapters.question: When does splitting work across sub-agents help, when does it destroy the task, and how can you tell in advance?
chapters.description: The public multi-agent disagreement resolved into a decision rule: the composability test, five topologies, the boundary problem and a sub-agent contract.
tldr: Two credible teams published opposite conclusions. Both are right, on different kinds of work.
Sub-agents are safe when their outputs combine without negotiation, and dangerous when they do not.
For coding, the default is one linear thread with disposable read-only scouts.
outcomes: Apply the four-question composability test before delegating
Choose a topology for a given task
Write a sub-agent contract that limits contract loss
Rank context boundaries by how much control you have over what crosses them
takeaways: Delegate read-mostly, additive work. Never delegate interlocking implementation or debugging.
If you cannot write the output schema in 20 lines, the work is not isolatable.
Isolation shrinks the parent's context and grows total spend.
A reset with a written handoff gives you more control than any compaction.

chapters.title: The tool surface: MCP, skills and progressive disclosure
chapters.question: How much context do tools, MCP servers and skills consume, and what does a healthy tool surface look like?
chapters.description: A tool-surface audit can reveal large definition waste. This chapter covers degradation curves, three architectures, a 30-minute audit, and a worked deletion-versus-deferral example.
tldr: Tool count hurts twice: definitions displace work, and more choices mean worse choices [S].
Deferred definitions fix displacement, not confusion. Only fewer tools fix confusion.
A 30-minute audit shows which tools were unused in your sample; delete only after a zero-call check.
outcomes: Separate displacement from selection confusion and pick the right fix
Compare eager, progressive and code-execution tool architectures
Run the six-step tool audit
Budget skills the same way you budget tools
takeaways: Treat about 20 active tools as a soft ceiling and about 40 as a hard one.
Zero-invocation tools are deletion candidates when the sample is representative; keep rollback.
Prefer the shell to an MCP server that duplicates it, unless the server is a deliberate security control.
Code execution removes a whole category of context and shapes results before they arrive.

chapters.title: Evaluating a context change
chapters.question: How do you prove a context-management change helped, with what statistical design, and at what cost?
chapters.description: Why context effects are hard to measure, twelve results that shape the design, Pass^k worked, sample sizes and a minimum viable experiment.
tldr: Context effects are small, fully tangled with the harness, and show up in variance first.
Run every task at least twice and report Pass² (solved both times), not single-run accuracy.
Pair your design and use McNemar's test: it needs roughly a third of the tasks.
outcomes: Explain why single-run accuracy is blind to compression damage
Compute Pass@k and Pass^k and read their ratio
Size an experiment honestly, or say that it is underpowered
Run a minimum viable paired experiment on your own tickets
takeaways: k = 2 is the minimum, because Pass² is the only way to see intermittency.
68% versus 74% on 50 tasks is not a result; the intervals overlap almost entirely.
Hold the compaction prompt constant; it alone can move results by 6.5 points.
Change one thing per experiment, and decide the stop rule before running.

chapters.title: Metrics and the real cost of context
chapters.question: What should you measure, and what does context really cost once the cache, latency and people are counted?
chapters.description: Twenty-six context metrics with the decision each drives, a four-line cost model, and the arithmetic that overturns two common cost beliefs.
tldr: Every metric should drive a decision. Five cover most of them.
Cost has four lines: compute, cache writes, latency and people. Most teams track one.
Cutting tokens can raise cost, and compaction saves far less money than its token count suggests.
outcomes: Choose the five metrics to track and the decision each drives
Compute cache-adjusted cost per turn
Work out when a compaction pays for itself
Use cost per solved task to compare configurations
takeaways: Stable prefix tokens cost about 0.10; churning tokens cost 1.25 every time they re-enter.
Compaction breaks even after about four turns; near the end of a session it is a pure loss.
You can over-compress as easily as over-load. Cost per solved task catches both.
When the next-dollar checklist comes up empty, stop optimising context.

chapters.title: Twenty-five hard calls
chapters.question: Which context decisions have no clean answer, and how do you decide them for your own situation?
chapters.description: Twenty-five context-management decisions with the tension, both sides, a recommendation and the conditions that flip it.
tldr: Twenty-five recurring decisions, each with both sides, a recommendation and what would flip it.
Almost every recommendation leans toward reversibility and explicitness, not cleverness.
The flip conditions are what make these re-decidable when your setup changes.
outcomes: Resolve the common trade-offs for your own setup
Recognise the conditions that flip each recommendation
Explain the pattern behind the recommendations
takeaways: Delete rather than select; redirect rather than filter; reset rather than compact.
Point rather than copy; keep exact strings verbatim; dereference rather than index.
When a context problem recurs, fix the repository, not the retriever.
Tier changes by reversibility: ship pure deletions, monitor structural changes, measure behavioural ones.

chapters.title: Forty-four failure modes
chapters.question: How does context management fail, what is the tell for each failure, and how do you contain it?
chapters.description: Forty-four context-management failures in eight clusters, each with its tell, detection, containment and fix, plus a symptom-to-cause index for incidents.
tldr: Forty-four failures in eight clusters, each with a tell, a detector, a containment and a fix.
Use the symptom index during an incident; read the clusters to prevent the next one.
Four questions asked before a long task pre-empt most of the list.
outcomes: Go from a symptom to its likely causes in under a minute
Contain a failure in-session and fix it permanently afterwards
Ask the four pre-emptive questions before a long task
takeaways: Starvation can survive review because the trajectory may look clean.
When a fact is poisoned, reset to before the poison; do not argue with it.
Cost rising after an "optimisation" usually means the cache broke.
"It worked yesterday" is a variance signal you never measured.

chapters.title: Sixteen antipatterns
chapters.question: What looks like good context hygiene but is not, and how do you tell the difference?
chapters.description: Sixteen practices that look like context hygiene and are not, each with the legitimate version, the tell, the cost and the fix, plus the three generators behind them.
tldr: Sixteen practices that imitate good hygiene, each with the tell that separates it from the real thing.
Three habits of mind generate almost all of them.
Fix the generator and you prevent the whole family.
outcomes: Spot each antipattern from its tell
Replace it with the legitimate version
Name the three generators and correct them at the source
takeaways: Treating the window as a container produces briefing documents, tool hoarding and token worship.
Adding feels like work; deleting looks like doing nothing. Make removal a reported result.
Measuring inputs instead of outcomes hides the harm you most need to see.

chapters.title: Eight case studies
chapters.question: What do these decisions look like on real, documented incidents, including ones where the change made things worse?
chapters.description: Eight context-management cases: two multi-agent outcomes, the summariser swing, compression and reliability, a cache disaster, category removal and a first audit.
tldr: Six cases are documented studies or incidents; two are labelled composites.
One change made things worse (dynamic tool loading) and one win came from removal (code execution).
Six of eight turned on what to remove or where to draw a boundary, not on a cleverer algorithm.
outcomes: Recognise the same patterns in your own incidents
Explain why the same architecture succeeded on research and failed on implementation
Use the cross-case patterns as a checklist
takeaways: Isolation succeeds or fails on composability, not on architecture.
The boundary component, such as the summariser, is a first-class quality lever.
Cache mechanics can invert the sign of a token optimisation.
The constructed audit separates waste from behaviour changes.

chapters.title: Your optimisation plan
chapters.question: Given everything so far, what exactly should I do, in what order, and when should I stop?
chapters.description: A sequenced seven-phase plan of about 16 hours, ordered by yield per effort, with a measurement gate per phase and an explicit stop rule.
tldr: Seven phases, about 16 hours over six weeks. Phases 0–2 take about seven hours and carry most of the benefit.
Every phase has a gate. Do not start the next phase until the gate passes.
Stop when the six stop-rule conditions hold. Past that, your constraint is elsewhere.
outcomes: Run the Phase 0 baseline and record eight numbers
Complete deletion and prevention in about five and a half hours
Know when a phase has worked and when to stop entirely
takeaways: The plan is ordered by yield per effort, not by intellectual interest.
Start with deletion when the audit finds dead or duplicate surface; keep it measured and reversible.
Measurement infrastructure is optional unless you will make several more changes.
Re-audit quarterly. Five of the six maintenance steps are deletions.

chapters.title: The diagnostic: score yourself, get one action
chapters.question: Where does my team stand on context management today, and what is the single next thing to do?
chapters.description: A 35-item self-audit across seven areas that produces a maturity level and exactly one next action, with a worked example and a one-question version.
tldr: Thirty-five items across seven areas, each scored 0, 1 or 2. Unknown scores zero.
Your level is the minimum across areas, not the average. Context fails at its weakest point.
The lowest area maps to exactly one next action.
outcomes: Score your setup in about 30 minutes
Read your level and your one next action
Recognise the most common failing shape: one strong area, the rest at zero
takeaways: Gating items cap an area, so polish cannot hide a missing foundation.
One action, not a programme. Re-score after it.
The one-question version covers most readers: what share of your context is tools you never call?

chapters.title: Sixty-two habits that compound
chapters.question: What small, daily practices pay for themselves, and when does each one apply?
chapters.description: Sixty-two concrete context-management habits for coding agents, ordered by when they apply, plus the eight that pay for themselves in the first week.
tldr: Sixty-two habits, ordered by when they apply: setup, opening, retrieval, state, boundaries, delegation, hygiene.
Eight of them pay for themselves in the first week, and five of those eight cost nothing.
The wins are mostly deletions and habits, not architecture.
outcomes: Apply the first-week eight today
Open, run and end a session with deliberate context habits
Keep the gains with a quarterly routine
takeaways: Spend 200 tokens on the opener: goal, paths, definition of done, what not to do.
Locate, then inspect, then read.
Compact after a test passes, never mid-debug; reset on the third repeated action.
When a context problem recurs, fix the repository.

chapters.title: The tooling landscape
chapters.question: Which open-source tools, plugins and local MCP servers improve context use, and which are worth adopting?
chapters.description: Open-source context tooling for coding agents across six layers, each with mechanism, cost and an adopt, trial, watch or skip verdict, plus a four-week starter stack.
tldr: Tools are grouped by the layer they act on: prevention, retrieval, tool surface, state, compaction, observability.
Verdicts are about categories. Named projects are examples to verify, not endorsements.
The highest-value action is often not installing anything.
outcomes: Pick a tool category for the layer that is your constraint
Adopt a four-week starter stack in the right order
Name what the ecosystem is still missing
takeaways: Check whether your harness already does it before installing anything.
Four shell wrappers usually beat any installed output-shaping tool.
Every memory tool needs a retrieval gate from day one.
Nothing off the shelf measures post-boundary re-fetch or Pass². You will have to build them.

chapters.label: A
chapters.title: Templates you can copy
chapters.question: What are the fill-in forms that make this operational, and which field in each carries the value?
chapters.description: Eight copyable templates for context management: budget audit, tool audit, plan file, compaction schema, handoff, sub-agent contract, postmortem and experiment spec.
chapters.visualExempt: Appendix of copyable templates; each template is a code block.
tldr: Eight standalone forms, each tied to a measured failure that happens when the decision is made implicitly.
If eight is too many, three carry most of the value: the budget audit, the compaction schema and the postmortem.
Every template has a copy button. Fill them in; do not file them.
outcomes: Copy the right template for the moment you are in
Know the one field in each that carries the value
takeaways: A form is a way to make a decision before you are under pressure to make it badly.
The compaction schema is the highest measured value per minute of effort in this research.
The postmortem's single question, was the decisive file ever in context, separates four failure classes.

chapters.label: B
chapters.title: Fifty-eight lessons, each falsifiable
chapters.question: What are the transferable lessons, why is each true, and what would prove each one wrong?
chapters.description: Fifty-eight numbered lessons on context management for coding agents, each with its mechanism and the observation that would falsify it.
chapters.visualExempt: Numbered reference list; the mechanisms are illustrated in the chapters each lesson links to.
tldr: Fifty-eight lessons in seven groups, each with a mechanism and a falsification condition.
A lesson you cannot falsify is a slogan, so each one says what would refute it.
Five matter most: budget not bucket, stable prefix, variance first, deletion first, and a stopping point.
outcomes: Cite a lesson with its mechanism
Test a lesson against your own workload
takeaways: It is a budget, not a bucket. Everything follows from that.
A large stable prefix beats a small churning one.
Compression damage is variance first. Measure Pass².
Deletion is often high-yield when the audit finds dead surface; context work has a stopping point.
